A lifeguard $L$ is watching a weather balloon $W$ rise vertically from a point $S$ on the beach. The point $S$ is $10\,\text{m}$ away from the lifeguard. If the balloon is rising at a constant speed of $1\,\text{m/s},$ determine the rate at which the angle of elevation $\theta $ formed by the lifeguard and the balloon is increasing at the moment when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Do not round the answer.

The angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/b4b48ffa8202e15042190b98b8fc11bb02bc06547abcfbfba87b1433e5161d9b.png)

  

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance between the lifeguard and the point on the beach directly beneath the balloon, and $y$ is the balloon's height. The quantity $x=10\,\text{m}$ does not change with time because the lifeguard does not move.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$
To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $y.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $y$ are the adjacent and opposite, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{10} \\ y & =10\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(10\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =10{sec}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=1$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{6}.$ Substituting these values into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =10{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =10{(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =10\cdot \frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ 1 & =\frac{40}{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{3}{40}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the angle of elevation is increasing at a rate of $\frac{3}{40}\,\text{rad/s}.$
